title: Long-run occupancy profiling playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a pragmatic playbook for long-run occupancy profiling of the serving runtime. The goal is to reliably push the system into a sustained throughput plateau and then characterize micro-variation, KV/cache decay effects, and tail behavior over multi-hour runs. Use this when you need production-grade throughput numbers (not smoke tests) or when investigating long-tail regressions that only appear after extended steady load.

Scope and expected outcomes:
- Produce stable throughput and latency curves for runs >= 30m (recommended 1–4h where feasible).
- Capture occupancy (in-flight requests, batch-size distribution, KV cache hit curve, GPU memory pressure) across time windows.
- Identify slow drifts (cache-utilization, allocator fragmentation, GC pauses, kernel warm/cold paths).
- Provide reproducible config artifacts and a runnable raw-trace for postmortem.

Quick rules of thumb:
- If you see >5% throughput drift over a 30m window, escalate; this indicates plateau instability.
- Prefer single-model, single-variant runs to remove routing noise.
- Keep background noise minimal: isolate hosts, freeze autoscaling, disable scheduled tasks.

Terminology used here:
- Occupancy: concurrent active requests or tokens being processed (not just QPS).
- Plateau: period where delivered throughput stays within +/-3% of median for at least 20 minutes.
- Cache decay: reduction in prefix/KV cache hit-rate over time due to eviction or key churn.

Experiment design checklist (pre-run) :
- Choose target arrival shape and sequence-length mix (see templates below).
- Pick run length: 60 minutes minimum; 2–4 hours preferred for cache-sensitive cases.
- Snapshot the exact model artifact/version and runtime kernel bundle (hash).
- Choose a reproducible RNG seed and record it.
- Prepare observability: Prometheus scrape intervals >=10s, traces enabled for 1% sampling.
- Disable autoscaler and any cross-region fallback.
- Ensure no other load generators are running on the same hosts.

Loadgen templates (YAML-style examples) :
-- template: steady_plateau_longrun
  description: uniform Poisson arrivals to reach a target sustained occupancy
  target_qps: 200
  concurrency_hint: 128
  arrival_distribution: poisson
  sequence_length_mix: 
    - {len: 32, pct: 50}
    - {len: 128, pct: 40}
    - {len: 512, pct: 10}
  prefix_cache_ratio: 0.6
  batch_timeout_ms: 6
  rng_seed: 987654321
  ramp_seconds: 300
  run_seconds: 7200

-- template: microburst-mix-injection
  description: baseline low qps + synthetic microbursts every 3m to test tail
  baseline_qps: 50
  burst_qps: 900
  burst_duration_s: 6
  inter_burst_interval_s: 180
  sequence_length: 128
  burst_pattern_seed: 42
  run_seconds: 3600

Notes on templates: the key knobs are arrival distribution, sequence mix, and batch_timeout_ms. Slightly increasing batch_timeout_ms (e.g. 6->8ms) moves more requests into larger batches — useful to validate batching economics but will change latency percentiles.

Priming and warmup guidance (practical, repeatable):
- Stage 1: soft ramp (ramp_seconds field) to avoid transient overloads. Use 3–10 minutes depending on target throughput.
- Stage 2: aggressive primer: run a 30s burst at 2x target QPS to fill caches and warm hot kernels.
- Stage 3: steady-mode entry: drop to target QPS and wait for 10–20 minutes to observe initial decay profile.
Record the time when you consider the run "in-plateau" (timestamp). All analysis windows should be relative to that timestamp.

Randomness and reproducibility fixes:
- Fix RNG seeds in both loadgen (pattern generation) and tokenizer (if applicable).
- Pre-tokenize inputs and store the byte arrays used in the run to remove tokenizer nondeterminism.
- Pin CUDA/cuDNN versions and report driver versions in the run manifest.
- Hash the binary artifacts: model checkpoint hash, runtime image digest.

Observability signals to collect (minimum):
- Request-level: request_id, arrival_ts, dispatch_ts, start_inference_ts, end_ts, chosen_batch_size
- Aggregates: tokens/sec, p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latency; qps
- Batching: batch_size distribution over time histogram
- Cache: KV-cache hit rate, prefix_hit_ratio, number of cached_keys
- Compute: GPU %util, SM efficiency, gpu_memory_used, GPU_power_watts
- OS: process_rss, page_faults, context_switches, cpu_steal
- Serving runtime: kernel_latency_ns per op type, allocator_fragmentation_ratio
- Traces: Sampler at 0.5–1% with full spans for slow requests > p99

Prometheus example queries to use in dashboards: (pseudocode)
- avg_over_time(tokens_per_second[5m])
- histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(batch_size_bucket[1m])) by (le))
- increase(kv_cache_hits_total[15m]) / increase(kv_cache_requests_total[15m])
- max_over_time(gpu_util_percent[10m])

Failure modes to watch for during long runs:
- Gradual cache hit-rate decline: correlates with rising latency and falling throughput — inspect eviction patterns and request key churn.
- Memory growth/fragmentation: look for monotonic process_rss increases; trigger heap dump and allocator profile.
- Kernel cold paths: repeated high-latency spikes aligned with small batch sizes may indicate unjitted kernels or suboptimal kernel selection.
- OS interference: periodic context-switch spikes or cpu_steal point to noisy neighbors.

Run-time mitigations (if mid-run):
- Reduce batch_timeout_ms to reduce latency at cost of throughput if Slack allows.
- Inject controlled cache refills (targeted prefixes) to measure hit-rate sensitivity.
- If memory grows, gracefully terminate and capture core dump + allocator profile.

Post-run analysis checklist:
- Validate plateau window: compute median throughput and confirm +/-3% stability for chosen window length.
- Compare first 10 minutes vs final 10 minutes to detect drift (tokens/sec, latency, kv-hit).
- Compute batch-size-weighted latency to rule out small-batch bias.
- Correlate p99+ spikes with traces and hardware counters (SM stalls, memcpy).
- Produce an experiment artifact: {config_hash, model_hash, kernel_bundle, start_ts, plateau_ts, csv_raw_metrics, traces_link}.

Example short run log (for traceability):
- start: 2025-05-12T09:00:00Z
- config: steady_plateau_longrun (seed=987654321)
- snapshot: model:v3.1.2 (sha256:abc123...), runtime: cudabundle-20250402 (sha256:def456...)
- ramped: reached target after 4m20s
- primer: 30s@2x at 09:04:00Z
- plateau declared: 09:14:30Z
- anomalies: cache_hit fell 0.08 -> 0.60 over 90m; long-tail p99.9 rose 40% near 09:57:xx
- artifacts: s3://rwd-bench/longrun/2025-05-12/ (metrics.csv, traces.zip, run_manifest.json)

Low-effort reproducibility snapshot (what to commit with a ticket):
- loadgen config file (YAML)
- pretokenized input sample (1000 items)
- model and runtime digests
- prometheus query set, dashboard snapshot link

Guidance for follow-ups and prioritization:
- If latency regression correlates with cache decline, prioritize cache eviction policy experiments and workload partitioning.
- If drift appears hardware-bound (SM efficiency down), schedule kernel selection re-profile and compare with a smaller seq-length corpus.
- If noise is environmental (cpu_steal, ctx switches), reproduce on isolated hosts and run again.

Appendix: small utilities and commands we use locally
- run loadgen: ./tools/loadgen --config runs/steady_plateau_longrun.yaml --out-dir /tmp/run-2025-05-12 --log-level info
- collect traces: ./tools/trace-collector --scan /tmp/run-2025-05-12 --out s3://rwd-bench/longrun/2025-05-12/traces.zip
- manifest hashing: sha256sum model.pt runtime.tar.gz > run_manifest.hash

Open questions for the next iteration:
- Default run length trade-off: is 2h enough for all cache-sensitive models or should we standardize on 4h?
- Should we add a controlled multi-tenant interference test harness to quantify neighbor-noise sensitivity?

Notes to self: keep this playbook lean — link to more prescriptive priming scripts rather than embedding them. Save one canonical template for microburst injection and one for long-run plateau.

End of playbook.
